fetch.title: fetch
fetch.plainEnglish: Open a filing cabinet. You tell it which drawer (logs, events, spans, bizevents) and it hands you every record in that drawer.
fetch.analogy: Like walking into a library and asking for every book in the Science section.
fetch.commonMistake: Forgetting that fetch must always be the first command. You cannot filter data you have not loaded yet.
fetch.tip: Always use a time range (from:-1h) in production so you do not pull millions of rows.

filter.title: filter
filter.plainEnglish: Throw away rows you do not care about. Only rows that match your condition stay in the pipeline.
filter.analogy: Like a sieve — only pebbles small enough to fall through the holes make it to the bottom.
filter.commonMistake: Using = instead of ==. In DQL, == means equality; = is only for assignments inside summarize or fieldsAdd.
filter.tip: Chain multiple conditions with and / or. Parentheses help when mixing them.

filterOut.title: filterOut
filterOut.plainEnglish: The opposite of filter. Remove rows that DO match your condition. Everything else stays.
filterOut.analogy: Like picking olives out of a salad — you remove the olives, everything else remains.
filterOut.commonMistake: Thinking filterOut removes the field. It removes the ROW, not the column.
filterOut.tip: Use filterOut when you want to exclude one noisy category (like INFO logs) and keep everything else.

summarize.title: summarize
summarize.plainEnglish: Crunch many rows down into a small summary table. You define what to calculate (count, sum, avg) and what to group by.
summarize.analogy: Like sorting a deck of cards into piles by suit, then counting how many cards are in each pile.
summarize.commonMistake: Forgetting the by:{field} clause. Without it, summarize collapses everything into one single row.
summarize.tip: You can compute multiple aggregations in one summarize: summarize total = sum(amount), count = count(), by:{product}

sort.title: sort
sort.plainEnglish: Reorder rows by a column. Use asc for smallest-first, desc for largest-first.
sort.analogy: Like arranging books on a shelf from thinnest to thickest.
sort.commonMistake: Sorting after limit. Always sort BEFORE limit, or you will cap the unordered list first.
sort.tip: During incidents, sort by count or duration desc — the worst offenders float to the top.

limit.title: limit
limit.plainEnglish: Keep only the first N rows. Discard everything after.
limit.analogy: Like taking only the first 10 photos from a roll of film.
limit.commonMistake: Using limit too early in the pipeline. If you limit before sorting, your top-N will be random.
limit.tip: Always place limit at the very end of your pipeline, after sort.

parse.title: parse
parse.plainEnglish: Pull structured fields out of unstructured text. You write a pattern that describes what the text looks like, and DPL extracts the values into named fields.
parse.analogy: Like using a stencil to trace shapes out of a messy drawing. The stencil defines the pattern; the traced shapes are your new fields.
parse.commonMistake: Writing a pattern that is too greedy. Use LD (lazy data) when the next literal in the pattern decides where a match stops.
parse.tip: Start small: extract one field first, test it, then add more matchers to the pattern.

fieldsAdd.title: fieldsAdd
fieldsAdd.plainEnglish: Create a new column by computing a value for every row.
fieldsAdd.analogy: Like adding a new column to a spreadsheet and filling it with a formula.
fieldsAdd.commonMistake: Trying to reference a field that does not exist yet. fieldsAdd can only use fields that are already in the pipeline.
fieldsAdd.tip: Use if() inside fieldsAdd to create categories: fieldsAdd tier = if(amount > 500, "premium", "standard")

fieldsRemove.title: fieldsRemove
fieldsRemove.plainEnglish: Drop one or more columns. The rows stay; only the specified fields disappear.
fieldsRemove.analogy: Like cutting out certain columns from a printed table before sharing it.
fieldsRemove.commonMistake: Removing a field you still need in a later command. DQL reads left-to-right; once removed, a field is gone.
fieldsRemove.tip: Use fieldsRemove to clean up verbose logs before exporting or sharing a report.

fieldsRename.title: fieldsRename
fieldsRename.plainEnglish: Change the name of an existing column.
fieldsRename.analogy: Like putting a new label on a folder without changing what is inside.
fieldsRename.commonMistake: Trying to rename a field that was never created. Make sure the field exists before renaming it.
fieldsRename.tip: Useful when merging data from different sources that use different naming conventions.

dedup.title: dedup
dedup.plainEnglish: Remove duplicate rows, keeping only the first occurrence for each value of a given field.
dedup.analogy: Like removing duplicate contacts from your phone — keep the first entry, skip the rest.
dedup.commonMistake: Expecting dedup to remove rows that are identical across ALL fields. It only checks the field you specify.
dedup.tip: After dedup, use fields to keep just the columns you need for a clean report.

makeTimeseries.title: makeTimeseries
makeTimeseries.plainEnglish: Group rows into time buckets and calculate a value for each bucket. Perfect for spotting trends and spikes.
makeTimeseries.analogy: Like counting how many cars pass through a toll booth every 15 minutes, then plotting those counts on a graph.
makeTimeseries.commonMistake: Forgetting the interval. Without interval:5m or similar, the command has no buckets to fill.
makeTimeseries.tip: Use by:{field} to create multiple time series on the same chart — one line per service or host.

expand.title: expand
expand.plainEnglish: Take an array field and turn each array element into its own row.
expand.analogy: Like taking a bag of marbles and placing each marble in its own cup.
expand.commonMistake: Using expand on a non-array field. If the field is a plain string, expand will create one row with the whole string.
expand.tip: After expand, you can filter on individual array values as if they were regular fields.

search.title: search
search.plainEnglish: Find rows that contain a specific word anywhere in any field.
search.analogy: Like using Ctrl+F on a document to find every mention of a keyword.
search.commonMistake: Expecting search to match exact field values. It searches across ALL fields, so results can be broad.
search.tip: Use search for exploratory hunting, then narrow down with filter once you know which field matters.
